help.intro: The Perfekt is how German talks about the past in conversation — 'I worked', 'I ate', 'I went' are all Ich habe gearbeitet, Ich habe gegessen, Ich bin gefahren. It is built from two pieces: a helper verb in the present (haben, or sein for a few verbs) in position 2, and the participle — ge- + stem + -t for regular verbs (gemacht, gelernt), ge- + stem + -en with a possible vowel change for irregular ones (gegessen, gefahren) — at the very end, exactly where a modal's infinitive goes. Fifteen verbs turn up in the Perfekt so often — in any story about yesterday or last weekend — that you need to recognise them straight away in what you hear and read. This quiz gives you those fifteen. The full system follows later in the course. Each sentence has two gaps: the helper verb in position 2 and the participle at the end — type both, one in each gap.
help.tips[0].title: haben + participle at the end
help.tips[0].text: Ich habe … gemacht. Er hat … gearbeitet. Wir haben … gegessen. The helper conjugates; the participle never changes and is the last word.
help.tips[0].examples[1].en: What did you do? – I read a book.
help.tips[0].check.q: We ate pizza yesterday: Wir ____ gestern Pizza gegessen.
help.tips[0].check.why: essen takes haben, and the helper agrees with wir: wir haben. The participle gegessen stays at the end.
help.tips[1].text: machen → gemacht, lernen → gelernt, fragen → gefragt, arbeiten → gearbeitet (extra e). essen → gegessen, lesen → gelesen, trinken → getrunken, schlafen → geschlafen, sehen → gesehen.
help.tips[1].examples[0].en: I learnt German and asked a lot.
help.tips[1].examples[1].en: He slept well and drank coffee.
help.tips[1].check.q: I asked my mother: Ich habe meine Mutter ____. (fragen)
help.tips[1].check.why: fragen is regular, so the participle is ge- + stem + -t: gefragt.
help.tips[2].title: Three to start with that take sein: fahren, bleiben, passieren
help.tips[2].text: Movement and change use sein instead of haben: Ich bin gefahren. Wir sind geblieben. Was ist passiert? Note also: no ge- on verbs ending in -ieren (passiert) or starting with ver- (verstanden).
help.tips[2].examples[0].en: I went to Berlin and stayed two days.
help.tips[2].examples[1].en: What happened? – I didn't understand anything.
help.tips[2].trap: English has only 'have'. 'Ich habe gefahren' is the error every English speaker makes; movers and changers take sein.
help.tips[2].check.q: On Monday I went to Cologne: Am Montag ____ ich nach Köln gefahren.
help.tips[2].check.why: fahren is a verb of movement, so it takes sein: ich bin gefahren.
help.tips[3].title: The bracket again
help.tips[3].text: Helper at 2, participle at the end — the same sandwich as the modal verbs. Everything you say about the past goes in the middle.
help.tips[3].examples[0].en: I ate at the café with Anna at the weekend.
help.tips[3].examples[1].en: We went to Hamburg on Sunday.
help.tips[3].check.q: Which sentence is correct? (She read a book in the evening.)
help.tips[3].check.why: The helper hat sits in position 2 and the participle gelesen closes the sentence; everything else goes in between.
help.remember[0]: ge- at the front, -t or -en at the back, and the whole word at the end of the sentence.
help.remember[1]: Movers and changers take sein: fahren, kommen, gehen, bleiben, passieren.
help.context.en: What did you do at the weekend? – I went to Hamburg. I saw my sister, we ate together and talked a lot. On Sunday I slept in. And you? What happened?
help.mistakes[1].why: The participle is the last word.
help.mistakes[2].why: -ieren verbs and ver-/be- verbs take no ge-.
help.hook: Tell someone what you did yesterday: ich habe gegessen, ich bin gefahren, with the past form landing at the end.
sentences[0].why: Regular Perfekt: haben + ge…(e)t — gearbeitet, with an extra e after the t-stem.
sentences[1].english: We stayed in Berlin for two days.
sentences[1].why: bleiben takes sein, not haben — staying counts as a change-of-state verb: sind … geblieben.
sentences[2].why: essen is irregular: hast … gegessen — with an extra g inside, gegessen.
sentences[3].english: At the weekend I went to Hamburg.
sentences[3].why: Movement from A to B takes sein: bin … gefahren.
sentences[4].why: fragen is regular: hat + ge…t — gefragt.
sentences[5].english: At first I didn't believe that.
sentences[5].why: glauben is regular: habe … geglaubt — ge + stem + t.
sentences[6].english: We were very lucky on holiday.
sentences[6].why: haben is its own helper: haben … gehabt.
sentences[7].english: Have you read the book yet?
sentences[7].why: lesen is irregular and keeps -en: Habt … gelesen.
sentences[9].english: What did you do on Sunday?
sentences[9].why: machen is regular: hast … gemacht — the Perfekt workhorse.
sentences[10].english: The baby slept very well today.
sentences[10].why: schlafen is irregular and keeps -en: hat … geschlafen — sleeping is no movement, so haben.
sentences[11].english: We have already seen the film.
sentences[12].why: passieren takes sein (something happened — a change), and verbs in -ieren take no ge-: ist … passiert.
sentences[13].english: I drank too much coffee today.
sentences[13].why: trinken is irregular with a vowel change: habe … getrunken — i → u.
sentences[14].why: Verbs starting with ver- take no ge-: habe … verstanden.
